hook: The graph of $y = \frac{1}{x^2}$ runs to the right forever, yet the region under it from $x = 1$ on has area exactly 1. The graph of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ looks almost the same, but the region under it has no finite area at all. An improper integral is how calculus decides which is which: as a limit.

figure.caption: Both curves approach 0, but the area under 1/x² from 1 to b levels off at 1 while the area under 1/x, ln b, keeps growing. The limit of the area decides convergence, not the height of the curve.

chain.cause: A limit of integration is infinite, or the integrand is unbounded on the interval
chain.effect: the integral is improper: it is not a definite integral in the old sense

chain.cause: Replace the troublesome end by a variable, $b$
Take the limit as $b$ approaches the troublesome end
chain.effect: if the limit is a finite number, the integral converges to it; otherwise it diverges

chain.cause: The integrand is unbounded at a point inside the interval
chain.effect: write it as two integrals that meet there, each one improper

ideas: $\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. It converges if this limit is a finite number and diverges otherwise.
Unbounded integrand at an end: $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = \lim_{a \to 0^+} \int_a^1 f(x)\,dx$. At an interior point, write it as two integrals that meet there.
Keep $\lim$ in every line until you take it; never substitute $\infty$ as a number.

misconception.right: An integrand approaching 0 does not decide anything. $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln b$, which grows without bound, so the integral diverges. Only the limit of the integrals decides.

summary: An improper integral has an infinite limit of integration or an integrand that is unbounded on the interval. Replace the bad end by a variable, integrate, and take the limit: a finite limit means the integral converges to that value; otherwise it diverges. Write the limit in every line, and break the interval at any interior point where the integrand blows up.
